blocks.text: A transgenic animal carries a foreign gene to make a desired protein. Transgenic animals are used to produce drugs, increase yields and increase resistance to disease, for example:

items: Transgenic dairy cows carrying human genes; the book says their milk is the same as human breast milk, though such cows make only some human milk proteins.
Transgenic goats whose milk contains strong spider-silk proteins.
Transgenic goats whose milk contains the human enzyme lysozyme, which fights diarrhoea-causing bacteria.
Transgenic fish with better growth, lower food intake, more cold tolerance and disease resistance.
Gene therapy, in which genetically modified viruses deliver genes to humans to treat inherited diseases such as faulty development of T and B cells and inherited blindness.
The first human drug from a transgenic goat, an anticoagulant that lowers the chance of blood clots during surgery or childbirth.
Malaria-resistant mosquitoes made in the laboratory with a gene that reduces the development of Plasmodium in them.

blocks.title: Tidbits
blocks.text: Foreign genes could in theory be put into germline or somatic cells of humans. Changes in germline cells would be inherited, so most research has focused on somatic cells because of the risks and ethical issues of germline changes. Since the mid-1980s transgenic mice have been a key model for studying disease, because their genome has been fully analysed and is very similar to the human genome.

blocks.prompt: Why does most human gene research use somatic cells rather than germline cells?
blocks.explanation: Germline changes would be passed to future generations, which raises risks and ethical problems; somatic changes affect only the treated person.

items: Transgenic animals: medicines in milk, silk proteins, faster-growing fish, malaria-resistant mosquitoes.
Gene therapy uses modified viruses; research focuses on somatic cells.
